title: Ephemeral Credential Discovery and Audit Packaging Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This playbook defines the procedures for discovering ephemeral credential exposure (short‑lived tokens, leaked API keys, temporary service account keys), containing active exposures, and assembling compliance-grade evidence packages suitable for SOC2/GDPR/ISO auditors. It covers detection signals, triage flows, forensic collection, RBAC remediation, audit-log correlation queries, data residency considerations, and packaging requirements for external audit requests.

Scope

- Applies to all ephemeral credentials issued by Redwood Inference services and cloud accounts (AWS, GCP, Azure) as well as internal service mesh tokens and third‑party integration secrets.
- Excludes long‑lived human user passwords handled by IDP MFA recovery flows (separate People Ops process).

Definitions

- Ephemeral credential: any non-human credential with a TTL <= 48 hours (examples: STS credentials, short-lived OAuth tokens, service account JSON keys with expiry, rotating API keys).
- Evidence bag: a zipped collection of immutable artifacts (logs, token metadata, rotation receipts, change control records) used to prove actions to auditors.
- Provenance record: chain of custody metadata for an artifact (collector, timestamp, hash, storage path).

Ownership and SLAs

- Incident owner: Security Oncall (primary).
- Evidence pack owner: Security Engineering (primary) + Platform SRE (secondary).
- Initial triage SLA: 30 minutes from detection to owner assignment.
- Evidence delivery SLA (to legal/compliance): 48 hours after containment for internal audits, 72 hours for external auditor requests (unless extended by legal).

Detection signals (priority order)

1. Audit-log anomalies: sudden burst of API tokens created or STS assume-role activity from unusual IPs or regions.
2. Alerting: IDS/EDR or custom detectors trigger on anomalous credential creation or high‑rate token exchange.
3. Third‑party notifications: vendor telemetry indicates credential exfiltration.
4. Internal telemetry: spike in failed auth attempts followed by successful token exchanges.

Triage checklist (executed immediately after owner assignment)

1. Identify credential type and scope: service account, user token, integration API key.
2. Map credential to issuing system and last known TTL/expiration.
3. Determine active usage: list IPs, regions, endpoints called, and last seen timestamps (from audit logs).
4. Classify impact: data access (none/limited/wide), production workload control, billing exposure.
5. If active abuse suspected, move to containment (next section).

Containment steps (ordered, do not skip)

1. Revoke or temporarily disable the credential at source: e.g., rotate API key, disable service account, or revoke token session. Commands: 
   - AWS (revoke STS session tokens via session policy + disable IAM role trust): aws iam update-assume-role-policy --role-name <role> --policy-document '<policy>'
   - GCP (disable service account key): gcloud iam service-accounts keys disable <KEY_ID> --iam-account=<SA_EMAIL>
   - Internal API key rotation (example): curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN' https://console.redwood.ai/api/v1/keys/<key-id>/rotate
2. If credential cannot be revoked immediately, create WAF/ingress deny rules to block known abusive IPs and associated sessions while preserving evidence.
3. Snap runtime state for forensic analysis (process lists, container metadata, in‑memory handles where permitted by policy). Use immutable snapshots to S3/GCS with encryption and hash manifests.
4. Notify affected product/service owners and create an incident timeline entry in the incident management system.

Evidence collection (core artifacts)

Provide the following artifacts in the evidence bag. Each artifact must include a provenance record (collector, UTC timestamp, sha256).

| Artifact | Format | Minimum retention | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Raw audit logs (ingest layer) | gz | 7 years (SOC2) | Include ingestion metadata and partition keys |
| Auth service audit events | jsonl | 7 years | Include request_id, token_id, issuer, expiry, principal |
| Token metadata snapshot | json | 7 years | token_id, created_at, expires_at, scopes, issuer |
| Network flows (pcap summary) | pcapng + metadata | 1 year | Full pcap only if legal approved |
| Rotation/disable commands | text | 7 years | console/API call logs showing who rotated/disabled |
| Change control ticket | pdf/html | 7 years | JIRA/Change approval record |
| Hash manifest | text | 7 years | sha256 for all artifacts |
| Chain-of-custody log | json | 7 years | Who accessed the bag and when |

For internal auditors a reduced evidence bag (no PCAPs) may be acceptable if legal approves.

Log correlation recipes (examples)

- BigQuery example (auth events):
  SELECT token_id, principal, issuer, event_time, action, source_ip
  FROM `redwood-prod.auth_events`
  WHERE token_id = '@{SUSPECT_TOKEN_ID}'
  ORDER BY event_time DESC

- Elasticsearch example (edge logs):
  GET /edge-logs/_search
  {
    "query": {
      "bool": {
        "must": [
          { "match": { "token.id": "SUSPECT_TOKEN_ID" } },
          { "range": { "@timestamp": { "gte": "now-7d" } } }
        ]
      }
    },
    "sort": [{"@timestamp":{"order":"desc"}}]
  }

- Cross‑service correlation: join auth_events.token_id -> edge_logs.token.id -> storage_access.object_key to show data touched. Export joins as CSV with column headers for auditors.

RBAC and entitlement remediation (post-containment)

1. Immediate: revoke affected credentials and perform targeted entitlement pruning.
2. Medium term (72h): run a privilege review for the role/identity and remove unused roles; implement just-in-time (JIT) activation for sensitive actions.
3. Long term: add a scheduled entitlement recertification for related roles and mark tickets for business owners to approve or decommission.

Secure SDLC integration (prevention and future-proofing)

- Require ephemeral credentials for all machine-to-machine integrations with TTL <= 24 hours where feasible.
- Enforce signing policies on artifact registries and require hashed manifests for CI outputs.
- CI/CD pipelines must emit audit events to the central auth_events topic; pipeline tokens are rotated automatically on pipeline completion.

Data residency and retention constraints

- When evidence contains personal data (PII), apply region-aware packaging: evidence generated in EU stays in EU storage buckets unless legal approves cross-border transfer.
- For GDPR Subject Access Requests that overlap with credential incidents, coordinate with Privacy and Legal to redact PII before external delivery.
- Retention minimums are aligned with SOC2 and internal policy: 7 years for auth and audit artifacts; shorter retention (1 year) for packet captures unless required for litigation.

Packaging the compliance evidence bag (step‑by‑step)

1. Assemble artifacts into a timestamped directory: evidence/<incident-id>/<utc-timestamp>/
2. Generate sha256 manifest and sign the manifest with the security evidence signing key. Example: openssl dgst -sha256 -sign /keys/evidence_signer.pem -out manifest.sig manifest.txt
3. Upload encrypted bundle to the evidence archive bucket with server-side encryption and object immutability tag (where supported).
4. Populate chain-of-custody log: collector name, tool, UTC time, artifact list, manifest hash.
5. Notify Compliance and Legal with secure link and attach a short executive summary (PDF) listing impact, key artifacts, and mitigation actions.

External auditor checklist (minimum items to include)

- Artifact manifest and signed hash
- Auth service audit events covering the attack window
- Evidence of credential rotation/disabling (API/console logs)
- Change control approval(s) for remediation actions
- Figure showing cross-service correlation of token use -> data/object access
- Proof of regional storage (if evidence contains PII)

Post-incident actions and continuous improvement

1. Root cause analysis within 7 days. Publish a redacted RCA to stakeholders.
2. Update auth anomaly detectors and add new rules if the exposure exploited a detection gap.
3. Run a tabletop focused on credential theft scenarios at the next game day.

Forensic and legal constraints

- Always consult Legal before sharing raw packet captures or PII outside the region.
- Chain-of-custody must be airtight for evidence to be admissible: avoid copying artifacts without recording a provenance entry.

Appendices

A. Example evidence manifest (text)
   incident_id: INC-2026-1987
   collected_by: security-oncall-1
   collected_at: 2026-02-18T14:12:03Z
   artifacts:
     - auth_events-20260218.gz sha256: 1a2b3c...
     - token-metadata-SUSPECT_TOKEN_ID.json sha256: f4e5d6...
   manifest_sha256: abcdef...

B. Quick utility scripts
- Rotate a key via the internal admin API (example):
  curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN' https://console.redwood.ai/api/v1/service-keys/rotate --data '{"key_id":"<KEY_ID>"}'

C. Contact list
